caveat: Figures are official data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) and the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the latest available for each measure. Public finance figures are provisional and routinely revised. Monthly borrowing is seasonal and should not be multiplied up to estimate a year.

metrics.metric_name: Public sector net debt (excluding public sector banks)
metrics.explanation: The headline measure of how much the UK government owes, after subtracting liquid assets. This is the main measure used in the monthly public finance statistics.
metrics.whatThisMeans: Think of it as everything the government has borrowed and not yet repaid, less the cash it holds. It is a stock, a total built up over many years, not a single year's spending. As a share of GDP this is around levels last seen in the early 1960s.
metrics.source_name: ONS, Public sector finances, UK: September 2026
metrics.notes: £3,005.0bn at end September 2026, the latest published cash figure and the first time net debt has exceeded £3 trillion, £91.7bn more than a year earlier. Excludes public sector banks. End-August was revised down £4.4bn to £2,981.2bn in this release, largely on updated Bank of England data, so debt rose £23.8bn over the month.

metrics.metric_name: Debt as a share of GDP
metrics.explanation: Net debt measured against the size of the economy for that period. This matters more than the cash total, because a bigger economy can support more debt.
metrics.whatThisMeans: If debt is around 94% of GDP, the government owes a little less than the economy produces in a year. Economists watch the trend in this ratio rather than the cash figure alone.
metrics.source_name: ONS, Public sector finances, UK: September 2026
metrics.notes: 94.0% of GDP at end September 2026, provisionally estimated, 0.7 percentage points lower than a year earlier, 1.2 points below the OBR forecast, and at levels last seen in the early 1960s. End-August was revised from 93.8% to 93.6% in this release. Over the past twelve months the ratio has stayed between 92% and 95% (October 2025 to September 2026, series HF6X: low 92.2% in January, high 94.5% in November and June).

metrics.explanation: Total net debt divided by the UK population. A way to picture the scale, not a bill anyone personally owes.
metrics.whatThisMeans: This does not mean each person owes this amount. Government debt is repaid through taxes and borrowing over time, not split between residents.
metrics.source_name: Calculated from ONS net debt and ONS population estimate
metrics.notes: Calculated at build time: net debt (£3,005bn) divided by population estimate (69.5m). Recomputed whenever either input changes.

metrics.explanation: What the government pays to service its debt over a year. Affected both by how much is owed and by the interest rate on it.
metrics.whatThisMeans: Interest is a real cash cost competing with other spending, around 8% of total public spending. Some of it rises and falls with inflation, because a share of UK debt is index-linked. On the narrower ONS measure described in the notes, central government net interest payable was £10.9 billion in September 2026 alone, so twelve such months do not add up to the figure above.
metrics.source_name: OBR, Economic and Fiscal Outlook March 2026 (central government debt interest, net of APF)
metrics.notes: £109.7bn in 2025-26 (OBR March 2026 forecast), 3.6% of GDP on the OBR's own basis. Includes the inflation uplift on index-linked gilts. The ONS outturn measure of central government net interest payable is narrower and lower, at £96.8bn for the same year on the October 2026 vintage (series NMFX).

metrics.explanation: How much the government borrowed in the latest month, the gap between what it spent and what it raised.
metrics.whatThisMeans: Borrowing is a flow (one period's gap), while debt is the stock that builds up over many periods. Monthly borrowing is seasonal (July is usually low, because self-assessment income tax lands that month), so it cannot be multiplied by 12 to get the year. Annual borrowing is around £134 billion.
metrics.source_name: ONS, Public sector finances, UK: September 2026
metrics.notes: £24.5bn in September 2026, £1.8bn more than September 2025 and £1.9bn above the OBR forecast, the second-highest September on record. Borrowing in the financial year to September was £97.8bn, £4.4bn less than the same period last year but £6.0bn above forecast. Excludes public sector banks.

gdp.notes: The nominal GDP consistent with the published debt-to-GDP ratio (net debt 3005.0 / 0.940). Calendar-year 2025 nominal GDP outturn is about £3,034bn; this measure is used for the translator's share-of-GDP figure.

population.notes: UK mid-2025 population estimate, 69,483,939 (ONS, Population estimates for the UK, mid-2025, published 1 October 2026).

adults.notes: Population aged 18 and over, UK mid-2025 estimate, 55,484,667, summed from single years of age 18 to 90 and over (ONS, Population estimates for the UK, mid-2025, table MYE2, published 1 October 2026). The same vintage as the population figure above.

taxpayers.notes: Number of income tax payers (HMRC, tax year 2023-24 outturn, published 15 July 2026). Later years are projections and run several million higher.

taxReceipts.notes: Central government total current receipts, financial year ending March 2026 (ONS). This is not the same as total tax receipts, which are lower at £1,108bn on a National Accounts basis (OBR March 2026), because it includes interest, dividends and other non-tax income. Total public sector current receipts are higher, around £1,235bn on the OBR March 2026 basis, against the £1,226bn the site derives as spending minus borrowing.
